papers.title: Accurate and scalable decontamination of imaging-based spatial transcriptomics via optimal transport
papers.summary: This paper presents a computational method that uses optimal transport theory to remove contamination from imaging-based spatial transcriptomics data, where signals from neighboring cells often leak into each other due to imperfect cell segmentation. The tool aims to be both accurate and scalable, meaning it can correct large, high-resolution spatial datasets without losing biological signal. This kind of decontamination step is crucial for ensuring that gene expression measurements attributed to a specific cell truly reflect that cell's biology rather than noise from its neighbors.
papers.why: Since this PhD project relies on spatial transcriptomics to accurately map gene expression in individual neurons and interneurons within complex brain tissue, reliable decontamination methods are essential for trustworthy downstream analysis of mitophagy, autophagy, and perineuronal net-related gene signatures.

papers.title: CoexpressDeconvolve enables reference-free single-cell-resolution deconvolution from spot-based spatial transcriptomics.
papers.summary: CoexpressDeconvolve is a computational tool designed to take spot-based spatial transcriptomics data, where each spot contains signals from multiple cells, and computationally break it down to single-cell resolution. Unlike many existing deconvolution methods, it does not require a pre-existing reference dataset of cell types, instead relying on gene co-expression patterns within the data itself. This reference-free approach could make it more flexible for studying tissues or cell populations that lack well-characterized reference profiles.
papers.why: This tool could help resolve the transcriptomic identity of rare or poorly annotated cell types such as interneuron subtypes and cells associated with perineuronal nets in spot-based spatial transcriptomics data without needing a pre-built reference.

papers.title: Integrated proteomics and network pharmacology reveal autophagy-lysosomal regulation underlying sulforaphane-mediated neuroprotection in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.summary: This study looks at sulforaphane, a natural plant compound, and how it might protect brain cells in Alzheimer's disease. Using proteomics (large-scale protein analysis) and network pharmacology (computational mapping of drug-target-disease interactions), the researchers identify pathways involved in its effects. They find that sulforaphane appears to work partly by regulating autophagy and lysosomal function, cellular processes responsible for clearing damaged components and toxic protein buildup.
papers.why: This paper is relevant because it connects autophagy-lysosomal pathway regulation to neuroprotection in a neurodegenerative disease context, directly relevant to the mitophagy/autophagy focus of the PhD project even though it lacks spatial or interneuron-specific data.

papers.title: Mitochondria-Lysosome Quality Flux in Aging Mesenchymal Stem/Stromal Cells: Quality-Control Bottlenecks and Therapeutic Opportunities for Regenerative Decline.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how the coordinated system of mitochondrial quality control and lysosomal degradation breaks down in aging mesenchymal stem/stromal cells (MSCs). It highlights specific bottlenecks in the mitophagy pathway, where damaged mitochondria fail to be efficiently cleared by lysosomes, contributing to reduced regenerative capacity. The authors also discuss potential therapeutic strategies to restore this quality control flux and improve stem cell function in aging or degenerative contexts.
papers.why: Although focused on stem cells rather than neurons, this paper's detailed mechanistic insights into mitochondria-lysosome quality control flux and mitophagy bottlenecks could inform conceptual frameworks or therapeutic targets relevant to neuronal mitophagy dysfunction in aging brains.

papers.title: Gut Microbiota and Aldosterone Regulate Natriuretic Peptide B Expression to Drive Mitophagy and Metabolic Reprogramming in Sepsis-Like Model of Myocardial Injury.
papers.summary: This study examines how gut microbiota and the hormone aldosterone influence natriuretic peptide B (NPPB) expression in a sepsis-like model of heart injury. The researchers show that this pathway triggers mitophagy (selective clearance of damaged mitochondria) and reprograms cellular metabolism in heart tissue. Their findings suggest a gut-heart axis where microbial and hormonal signals converge to control mitochondrial quality control during systemic inflammation.
papers.why: While this paper focuses on cardiac tissue rather than neurons, its detailed characterization of mitophagy regulation and metabolic reprogramming mechanisms could offer conceptual parallels or methodological insights applicable to studying similar processes in brain cells.

papers.title: Autophagy in the Regulation of Placental Development: From Trophoblast Differentiation to Metabolic Stress Adaptation
papers.summary: This paper reviews how autophagy supports placental development by regulating trophoblast cell differentiation and function. It discusses how autophagy helps placental cells adapt to metabolic stress conditions like hypoxia and nutrient deprivation during pregnancy. The review likely covers molecular pathways linking autophagy to placental health and pregnancy complications.
papers.why: While this paper focuses on autophagy, its context is placental biology rather than neuronal mitophagy or brain-related autophagy mechanisms, making it largely tangential to the core research profile.

papers.title: 5-Fluorouracil-based chemotherapy disrupts autophagy flux and protein synthesis in cultured myotubes: a role for mTORC1 signaling.
papers.summary: This study looked at how 5-Fluorouracil, a common chemotherapy drug, affects muscle cells (myotubes) grown in culture. The researchers found that the drug disrupts autophagy flux, the process cells use to recycle damaged components, and also impairs protein synthesis. They identified mTORC1 signaling, a key regulator of cell growth and metabolism, as playing a role in these disruptions.
papers.why: While this paper focuses on muscle cells rather than neurons, its insights into autophagy flux disruption and mTORC1 signaling could offer mechanistic parallels relevant to understanding autophagy and mitophagy dysregulation in neurons.

papers.title: The crosstalk between sequestosome 1 and heme oxygenase-1 in regulating autophagy/oxidative stress in bovine mammary epithelial cells.
papers.summary: This study looks at bovine mammary epithelial cells and how two proteins, sequestosome 1 (p62/SQSTM1) and heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), interact to regulate autophagy and oxidative stress responses. SQSTM1 is a well-known autophagy receptor protein, while HO-1 is a stress-response enzyme involved in managing oxidative damage. The paper likely explores how these two pathways communicate to protect mammary cells under stress conditions.
papers.why: Although this paper is in mammary cells rather than neurons, the core molecular players (SQSTM1/p62-mediated autophagy and oxidative stress crosstalk) are directly relevant to understanding mitophagy/autophagy regulatory mechanisms that may translate to neuronal contexts.
